claim: Uniform swing satisfies the mean-swing condition (A1) and party-neutrality (A3) but violates the bounds condition (A2): it can predict vote shares outside [0,1] whenever a district's prior vote share plus the aggregate swing would exceed 100% or fall below 0%.
stance_target: uniform swing is a logically well-behaved model of inter-election vote change
scope_conditions: general axiomatic model of two-party district-level swing
quoted_support: Although it is easily seen that Uniform Swing satisfies (a1) and (a3), it does not satisfy (a2).

claim: Proportional swing satisfies the mean-swing condition (A1) but violates both the bounds condition (A2) and the party-neutrality condition (A3).
stance_target: proportional swing is a logically well-behaved model of inter-election vote change
scope_conditions: general axiomatic model of two-party district-level swing
quoted_support: It is easily veriﬁed that Proportional Swing does satisfy (A1)... This causes a violation of the bounds condition (A2) and also shows that (A3) fails.

claim: No swing model that is linear in the aggregate swing term s can simultaneously satisfy the mean-swing condition (A1) and the bounds condition (A2) -- a formal impossibility result (Proposition 2.7) covering the entire family of models that includes both uniform and proportional swing.
stance_target: some linear-in-swing model exists that avoids both the mean-swing and bounds violations of uniform/proportional swing
scope_conditions: general axiomatic model of two-party district-level swing, models linear in aggregate swing s
quoted_support: Proposition 2.7. No swing model linear in s can satisfy both (A1) and (A2).

claim: The authors construct a piecewise-linear swing model (f = s(1-x_i)/(1-x-bar) for s>=0, else s*x_i/x-bar) that satisfies all three axioms (mean-swing, bounds, neutrality) simultaneously and describe it as the simplest functional form achieving this.
stance_target: a logically consistent alternative to uniform and proportional swing exists and is tractable
scope_conditions: general axiomatic model of two-party district-level swing
quoted_support: Straightforward algebra shows that this model satisfies (A1), (A2) and (A3). This is the simplest functional form we can ﬁnd for which which (A1)–(A3) are satisﬁed.

claim: On tens of thousands of paired U.S. congressional elections 1968-2016, all three swing models (uniform, proportional, piecewise) achieve winner-prediction accuracy around 85-95% and correlation above 80%, but all perform poorly at predicting the SIGN of district-level swing, often scoring near or below 50% (worse than a coin flip) depending on the uncontested-district convention used.
stance_target: swing models reliably predict the direction of district-level change, not just the aggregate winner
scope_conditions: U.S. congressional elections 1968-2016 paired adjacent elections, dataset from Katz et al. (2020)
quoted_support: all models had difﬁculty in predicting the sign of district-level swings, scoring around 50% or even substantially lower, worse than ﬂipping a coin, in some scenarios.

claim: In close U.S. congressional races (winner scoring 50-52.5% of the two-party vote), all swing models perform much worse: winner-prediction accuracy drops to only ~57-58% and correlation between predicted and actual results drops to just ~20-22%.
stance_target: swing methods retain useful accuracy in close/competitive electoral units
scope_conditions: U.S. congressional elections 1968-2016, close races defined as 50-52.5% winner margin
quoted_support: All measures performed relatively poorly in this case at predicting the winner, scoring only around 57% — as expected, close races are harder to call. Although they did better on predicting the sign of the district-level swing, the correlation dropped to just over 20%.

claim: The convention chosen for coding uncontested/uncompetitive districts (e.g. as 100% for the winner vs. an ad hoc 75%-25% split) has a large, measurable effect on the accuracy scores of all swing models, meaning published fit statistics for uniform/proportional swing are highly sensitive to this often under-documented data-processing choice.
stance_target: reported goodness-of-fit for uniform/proportional swing models is contingent on ad hoc uncontested-district recoding decisions
quoted_support: As we show empirically with data from U.S. congressional elections, the choice of such correction makes a substantial difference to results.
numbers: 75% commonly imputed value for uncontested-district winner

claim: The 'paradox of swing' -- that uniform swing has an amazingly good empirical fit to British and U.S. election data despite weak theoretical grounding -- was named and discussed by Butler and Stokes (1969) and has persisted as an unresolved puzzle for decades.
stance_target: why uniform swing works well empirically despite theoretical objections
scope_conditions: British and U.S. elections, post-WWII British National Election Study series
quoted_support: The remarkable empirical ﬁt of uniform swing led Butler and Stokes (1969) to talk about the “paradox of swing”.

claim: The uniform swing model was first applied to British elections by David Butler; its use for multi-party systems by focusing on the top-two-party contest was promoted in the U.S. context by Butler and Van Beek (1990).
stance_target: origin and diffusion history of the uniform swing model
scope_conditions: United Kingdom and United States electoral analysis
quoted_support: Butler, in a chapter in McCallum and Readman (1999, pp. 263–265) is credited with ﬁrst using uniform swing to model British elections... The use of the uniform swing model was promoted by Butler and Van Beek (1990) and is now common in the U.S.

claim: Proportional swing was likely first proposed by Berrington (1965) as an alternative to uniform swing and has since become the main rival model in the literature.
stance_target: origin of the proportional swing model
quoted_support: We believe that this model was ﬁrst proposed by Berrington (1965), where it was offered as an alternative to uniform swing.

claim: The authors argue that both a purely statistical/machine-learning approach and existing swing models are limited by the small total number of historical elections available for training/validation, which should temper confidence in out-of-sample forecasting performance.
stance_target: reliability of data-driven (including ML) electoral forecasting models given limited historical sample sizes
quoted_support: The total number of political elections in human history is not large compared to the enormous corpuses typical in areas considered to be machine learning success stories.

claim: A mean-reversion term can be added to any of the axiom-satisfying swing models (h(x_i, x-bar) = c(x-bar - x_i), c>0) to allow districts with no aggregate swing to still change, reflecting the empirical observation that extreme prior vote shares tend to revert even absent an aggregate national swing.
stance_target: swing models should incorporate reversion to the mean rather than assuming zero-swing districts are static
quoted_support: This condition says that when there is no aggregate swing, our best predictor of outcomes in individual districts is that they will be unchanged from the previous period. We do not regard this as a desirable property to impose generally on inter-election swing.

claim: The authors explicitly flag that their models assume swing moves identically across all districts relative to the polity as a whole, an assumption violated by simultaneous but geographically differentiated realignment trends (e.g. rural areas shifting one direction while suburban areas shift another) -- a limitation directly relevant to projecting local French swing under a nationally-uneven RN dynamic.
stance_target: swing models correctly capture geographically differentiated realignment dynamics
scope_conditions: general axiomatic swing model, future-work discussion
quoted_support: we assume that swing moves in the same way in each of the districts as it does for the polity as a whole. But that assumption is violated if, for example, there is a simultaneous realigning trend that works differently in different parts of the country, e.g. rural areas shifting Republican while suburban areas [shift Democratic]

claim: The piecewise model achieves perfect (100%) bounds-compliance across every dataset and quartile subset tested, while uniform and proportional swing violate bounds in 83-100% of cases depending on the uncontested-district coding convention, most severely (as low as ~83% compliance) under the strictest 'winner takes 100%' convention.
stance_target: the piecewise model has a decisive practical advantage over uniform/proportional swing in avoiding logically impossible predictions
scope_conditions: U.S. congressional elections 1968-2016, Katz et al. (2020) dataset, unc1.0 coding convention
numbers: piecewise bounds compliance 1.000 in every reported subset
uniform bounds compliance as low as 0.832 (unc1.0, full dataset)
uniform bounds compliance as low as 0.816-0.857 in swing-quartile subsets
